Blackhawkfx wrote: By trading based on M15/M30, definitely there are plenty of opportunity on daily bases but it's all drill down to the skill of the trader himself. I remember the pros always mentioned risk only 1-2% per trade but I've different mindset.

It's all drill down to the accuracy of the trader on winning probability. No matter 1% or 5% risk per trade. Its financial psychology + skillset that keep the traders at the winning side. I've witnessed a trader's account with consistency trading 5% risk per trade for 6 years with very consistency results.

Financial stability + good skillset + trading plan = Trading success. Do you agree?

BH

Yes I agree. If you're confident in your ability, and are able to produce consistent results - and crucially able to handle the mental anguish that might come with losing a few in a row at high risk levels, then you should go for it. It's definitely not for everyone though.

At this stage, I'm looking for consistency to lose no more than 1 in 5 trades. Still not quite there yet - I had a few good runs last week, but I've sat down today, "rusty" from not trading for a couple of days, and made some daft trades, trying to TT levels with no real confirmation on M1.

When I can hit that level, I will be compounding my winnings on the day. As soon as I make 10% profit on the day, I'll start putting 10% risk on my trades. If I lose - no biggie, I'm just back to where I started for the day, and will drop back down to initial risk. If I go on a good winning run however, it'll make savage account gains in a short space of time.

Quick something I knocked up to monitor my average position when adding to a trade in progress, and show me where multiplying my total lots by a factor of x will put my average position. It moves up and down as the bid price moves up and down. The idea is that I wait for a sufficiently deep retrace that I can double my lots (or whatever) and keep my average position behind a "safe" extreme - typically a FTR, the engulfing of which would mean I would consider the trade dead in the water.

Once a trade is in progress and you double (or whatever) up, you essentially go double or quits. You're either out for a lot more at your target, or you lose the lot at B/E at your new average position level if price reaches it.

It's a concept called "Space management" I found on another forum some time ago. The idea isn't new of course. If you're feeling really bold, and your trade has run almost all the way to target, you can do something silly like x10 your lots for the final stretch, "compressing" your space. You can also remove lots to a trade in progress if it looks like it's getting into trouble, putting some in the bank, and moving your average position further out, "expanding" your space, and giving yourself more room to survive a deep RT. If the RT ends up continuing back in your original trade direction, you can "compress" the space back again.

It's more suited for swing or position type trades I think, running over many hours, days, or even weeks, but you can still use it on a LTF trade, as I am attempting to do here.

Something I hope to master, is if I get on something that goes on a good run over several hours, is to "compress" up my space upon every successful retest and hold of freshly created FLs after engulfs.

Unfortunately all the fancy position management tools in the world can't guard against idiocy. I doubled up too soon, losing my position, instead of waiting for the retest of the FL. Oh well, live and learn... (slowly it seems).

Playing around with my composite index code, I thought it might be interesting to create a composite "index" index - comprised of the FTSE, DAX, S&P and Dow - just to see if it was possible to detect any moves brewing. Quite often we seem to see these indexes move in sync with one another, with the strength of the moves varying to one degree or another.

Many of the candles are blurred and fuzzy, which represents times in which the indices were moving around out of sync with one another. However, at other times, clear moves appear on the index, showing us that co-ordinated buying or selling was taking place across all 4.

At 1830ish yesterday, we can see the following setup on this "index" index, which came to and end at about 1400 today:

And here, I'm going to show the FTSE, DAX, S&P and Dow (in that order) with the same two time periods marked:

Pretty neat huh? To think, each one of these indexes is itself a weighted representation of at least 30 share prices, or 100 or 500 share prices in the case of two of them. So in order for a composite index created from these 4 to all move in sync like this, it means that co-ordinated buying and selling of 100s of shares is going on across 3 different countries at very precise times. And some people say the market is random...

Hopefully I can use this moving forwards to give me some good heads up on when the indexes are about to shift. Now that my chart reading skills have improved quite a bit, I'm planning to start looking at my GBPX, JPYX etc indices again. I'd dropped them for a while because they were confusing me - they behave almost like normal pairings in the moves that they make, but sometimes a little oddly.
